Hochstrasser, in Vattel, The Law of Nations, ed. Béla Kapossy and Richard Whatmore (Indianapolis: Liberty Fund, 2008), pp. 747–772. The translation follows the text appended to Pradier-Fodéré's edition of Le droit des gens (Paris 1863), not the 1747 print. The editors' notes are left out.

sents: Natural laws, natural jurisprudence, and moral science are three things that are often confused in ordinary language because they all three have the same object: to know how to order the customs and conduct of men.
But in handling a topic clearly and securely it is necessary to separate out carefully those issues that are in reality distinct.

flags.fr: savoir, de  régler
flags.en: to know how to order
flags.note: 'savoir' here means 'namely' (all three have the same object, namely to regulate men's morals and conduct); the English reads it as the verb 'to know', so the shared object becomes knowing how to order conduct rather than regulating it.

flags.fr: les mœurs
flags.en: the customs
flags.note: 'mœurs' means morals or moral manners (the subject of the 'science des mœurs' of §4); 'customs' suggests social convention and loses the moral sense.

sents: A law is in general a rule by which we are obliged to determine our actions; and natural laws, in particular, are those that we derive from nature, or whose rationale is found in the essence and nature of man, and of things in general.
Natural jurisprudence is a general theory of the duties of man, considered simply as man, or a science, which teaches us what is naturally good or bad in man, what he must and must not do.

flags.fr: ce qui est naturellement bon, ou mauvais à l'homme
flags.en: what is naturally good or bad in man
flags.note: Literally 'what is naturally good or bad for man' (what benefits or harms him); 'in man' turns Vattel's perfectionist good-for-man into qualities found in man.

sents: Moral science or ethics is a practical science, which teaches us how we should direct our faculties to practice what is good, and avoid what is bad.
Often the term moral science is employed to designate the study of behavior in general, and in this sense it includes natural law and ethics.

Sometimes moral science seems to mean the theory of our duties, insofar as we are obliged to employ them, for ourselves, as rational creatures; and natural law includes the theory of these same duties insofar as we are bound to them in respect of other men, as members of human society, or as others have the right to require that we observe them.
But our distinction (§III) is more tidy and convenient, and it contains everything, for natural law comprises also our duties toward ourselves.

flags.fr: le Droit Naturel
flags.en: natural law
flags.note: 'Droit Naturel' was rendered 'natural jurisprudence' in §§1 and 3 to keep it apart from 'Loix Naturelles' (natural laws); from here on the English switches to 'natural law', blurring the three-way distinction (natural laws / droit naturel / morale) Vattel has just drawn, and the same words later also render 'la loi naturelle'.

flags.fr: notre distinction
flags.en: (§III)
flags.note: The cross-reference '(§III)' is not in the 1747 text; it probably comes from the 1863 Pradier-Fodéré reprint or the translator.

sents: With that established, we look for the foundation of natural law, and the principle which compels us to practice what it prescribes for us, and avoid what it forbids us.
On these two points there have been major disputes among the learned.

flags.fr: le principe qui nous oblige
flags.en: the principle which compels us
flags.note: Literally 'the principle that obliges us'; 'compels' suggests physical or coercive necessity, whereas the essay is precisely about the principle of (moral) obligation.

sents: If by the foundation of natural law we understand the source from which can be derived the rules and precepts; the principle in which is found what can provide an explanation for why these rules and precepts are as they are, then we would not wish to look further than in the essence and nature of man and things in general.

For, since natural law is the science which tells us what is naturally good or bad in man (§III), how shall we determine what is naturally good or bad for him, if not through his essence and nature, and by the nature and essence of things, through considering the degree of suitability between actions and this essence and this nature?
This truth is conﬁrmed a posteriori or by experience.

To determine whether someone has given an accurate idea of the laws of nature, examine what there is in man and in other things that is in accordance with their essence and nature, and you will see how you will understand clearly from that why our free actions must be regulated and determined in the manner that natural law prescribes.
It would be easy to give examples of this.
But each person can put this to the test for himself.
notes: See Wolff, Phil. Pract. Univ., part I, §cxxxvii.

flags.fr: on ne sauroit chercher ce fondement ailleurs que
flags.en: we would not wish to look further than
flags.note: Literally 'one could not look for this foundation anywhere but'; the French states an impossibility, the English only a preference.

flags.fr: ce qui est naturellement bon ou mauvais à l'homme
flags.en: what is naturally good or bad in man
flags.note: Literally 'what is naturally good or bad for man', as the English itself renders the same phrase later in the sentence ('good or bad for him'); 'in man' changes the notion of the good.

flags.fr: la convenance, ou la disconvenance des actions
flags.en: the degree of suitability between actions
flags.note: Literally 'the agreement or disagreement of actions' with man's essence and nature; the English folds the pair into a graded 'degree of suitability', and the key term is rendered differently in §7 ('harmony or disharmony') and §9 ('aptness or inappropriateness').

flags.fr: Que quelqu'un vous ait donné une juste idée des loix de la nature
flags.en: To determine whether someone has given an accurate idea of the laws of nature
flags.note: Literally 'Suppose someone has given you an accurate idea of the laws of nature' (then examine man's nature and you will see why they hold); the English turns the a posteriori confirmation of the foundation into a test of whether someone's account is accurate.

sents: All the authors of different systems are obliged to agree with what we have just established, whatever their sense may be of the principle of obligation, which we shall speak of presently.

Those who delude themselves that natural law was invented for the beneﬁt of human society, must agree that the source of this view can only be the nature and essence of things and of man in particular.

For, I ask you, where could these would-be inventors have learned with such certainty that some actions are useful to the human race and that others are harmful, if not by considering the harmony or disharmony of these actions with the nature of man and the nature of things?
Therefore it is on this nature that they have had to base their whole theory of rules and the laws of natural jurisprudence.

flags.fr: s'imaginent
flags.en: delude themselves
flags.note: Literally 'imagine' or 'suppose'; 'delude themselves' makes Vattel's mild scepticism about the utility theorists an outright charge of self-deception.

flags.fr: pour l'utilité de la société humaine
flags.en: for the beneﬁt of human society
flags.note: Literally 'for the utility of human society'; 'benefit' hides the technical term 'utilité' that ties the passage to the utility doctrine (Carneades, Hobbes) Vattel is answering.

flags.fr: la source d'où on l'a puisé
flags.en: the source of this view
flags.note: Literally 'the source from which it [natural law] was drawn'; the English makes nature the source of the utilitarians' view rather than of natural law itself, which is the point of the argument.

flags.fr: avec quelque certitude
flags.en: with such certainty
flags.note: Literally 'with any certainty'; the English implies they did attain great certainty, whereas Vattel asks how they could have had any certainty at all without consulting nature.

flags.fr: utiles à la société humaine
flags.en: useful to the human race
flags.note: Literally 'useful to human society' (as rendered in the previous sentence); 'human race' drops the social frame of the utility argument.

flags.fr: la convenance ou la disconvenance
flags.en: the harmony or disharmony
flags.note: Literally 'the agreement or disagreement'; the key term convenance/disconvenance is rendered differently here than in §6 ('degree of suitability') and §9 ('aptness or inappropriateness').

sents: The same must be said of those who assign the instituting of natural law to the arbitrary will of God.

For, at the same time as they recognize God as a wise being, who ordains nothing without wisdom, they must agree that God could only give laws suitable to the nature of things, and particularly to the essence and nature of man, whom he instructs to observe them; laws whose rationale is found in this essence and nature.
We can go further: how do these authors know that God has laid down such-and-such laws rather than others quite contrary to them?

Doubtless it is because knowing that God is a wise being, they consider, rightly, that he could only give laws that are the most appropriate to man, the most advantageous to the good of society in general, and to that of each individual in particular.
But how will they know these most advantageous of laws?
They will consider the nature of man and things, and they will see which laws are most appropriate to them.
They are required to draw on the same source as us.
This is sufﬁcient to show that natural law is founded on the essence and nature of things and of men in particular.
Cicero recognized this when he said that law is established by nature: natura ipsa constitutum est jus.
We attain knowledge of these laws through reason.

This faculty of the soul teaches us what is the essence and nature of man and of things in general, and makes us see the aptness or inappropriateness of actions in relation to this essence and nature: from this we derive general rules or laws which constitute the body of natural jurisprudence.

flags.fr: la convenance ou la disconvenance des actions
flags.en: the aptness or inappropriateness of actions
flags.note: Literally 'the agreement or disagreement of actions'; a third rendering of the key pair convenance/disconvenance (cf. §6, §7), so the English reader cannot track the concept.

sents: But it is not enough that these laws exist and that they are known: for men to be obliged to obey them they must also be effective.
Everyone agrees that they are so bound, but authors disagree on the principle of this obligation.
Some derive it from the authority of a superior, which can only be God, the author of nature; others base it on the very beauty of virtue, which, by its nature, is preferable to vice.
Finally, others say that man, being a rational and sociable creature, must act in conformity with this character.
Let us try to determine the true and ﬁrst principle of this obligation and reveal where all these authors agree and are right, and where their views err.
To succeed in this it is absolutely necessary to develop a clear and distinct idea of things, and to provide good deﬁnitions.

We shall see that it is as a result of having neglected this rule that clever authors have caused themselves so much embarrassment in this matter, and have seemed to fall into views that are so mutually opposed.

flags.fr: il faut encore pour qu'elles se trouvent efficaces, que les hommes soient  obligés de les observer
flags.en: for men to be obliged to obey them they must also be effective
flags.note: Literally 'for them to be effective, it is further necessary that men be obliged to observe them'; the English inverts the relation, making efficacy the condition of obligation instead of obligation the condition of the laws' efficacy, which sets up the whole inquiry into the principle of obligation.

flags.fr: se sont si fort embarrassés
flags.en: have caused themselves so much embarrassment
flags.note: 's'embarrasser' means to get entangled or confused; modern 'embarrassment' (social awkwardness) misleads: Vattel says the authors tied themselves in knots.

sents: To determine what obligation is requires ﬁrst an examination of what is commonly understood when this term is employed.

Ask any man who says, “We are obliged to do something,” and you will see that he means that we are under a kind of necessity to do this very thing; that we are compelled, bound, tied—as if forced—although not forced or constrained physically by an external cause that acts violently upon us, but morally, and in a way that free beings can be engaged to do something even against the urging of their passions.
Now, what are the reasons which bring free beings to act even against their inclination, without physical compulsion or external causes?

They can only be motives, which being immediate to the soul, perceived and evaluated by reason, make us feel the necessity of acting in such a fashion and resolve the will, often against the heart’s inclination and despite the resistance of the passions.
How therefore are we compelled to take a certain action?
It is through the linkage of a powerful motive with this action.

Thus, there are two issues to consider in respect of obligation: 1. The principle which gives birth to or which constitutes it, which creates the obligation; 2. The condition in which we ﬁnd ourselves when we are so obligated.

flags.fr: Or quelles sont ces choses
flags.en: what are the reasons
flags.note: Literally 'what are these things'; 'reasons' anticipates the answer and blurs Vattel's distinction between motives (motifs), named in the next sentence, and reason (raison), the faculty that weighs them.

flags.fr: étant présens à l'ame
flags.en: being immediate to the soul
flags.note: Literally 'being present to the soul (mind)'; 'immediate' suggests that motives act directly and without mediation, whereas Vattel says only that they are before the mind, to be perceived and weighed by reason.

flags.fr: Comment sommes-nous donc obligés
flags.en: How therefore are we compelled
flags.note: Literally 'how then are we obliged'; rendering 'obligés' as 'compelled' brings back the language of constraint that Vattel has just excluded from moral obligation ('not forced or constrained physically').

sents: Hence it follows that obligation is characterized as active and passive.
Active obligation is the connection of the motive with the action.
Passive obligation is a moral necessity to act or not to act.
The former is the principle which sways the intelligent being, and the latter is the condition in which this being ﬁnds himself.
Passive obligation produces active obligation just as cause gives birth to effect.
For, if it is morally necessary to act, it is necessary to wish to act.

Now, there is no will in the soul without motivation; therefore to bring about the moral necessity to undertake a particular action, some motivation must be linked to this action, which you cannot separate from it.

flags.fr: L'obligation passive naît de l'obligation active, comme l'effet naît de la cause.
flags.en: Passive obligation produces active obligation just as cause gives birth to effect.
flags.note: Literally 'passive obligation arises from active obligation as the effect arises from the cause'; the English reverses the causal order, making passive obligation the source of active obligation, against Vattel's definitions and the proof that follows.

flags.fr: il est nécessaire que vous vouliez agir
flags.en: it is necessary to wish to act
flags.note: Literally 'it is necessary that you will to act'; 'wish' weakens the act of willing (vouloir) to a mere desire and breaks the link with 'volition' in the next sentence.

flags.fr: il ne se forme point de volition dans l'ame sans motif
flags.en: there is no will in the soul without motivation
flags.note: Literally 'no volition is formed in the soul without a motive'; the English makes the will itself (the faculty) depend on motivation rather than each act of willing, and replaces the defined term 'motive' with the vaguer 'motivation' (also in 'some motivation must be linked').

sents: There is good reason why we pause to demonstrate this origin for passive obligation.

It proves the reality of our deﬁnition and shows that we are in agreement with the most famous writers, though sometimes with this difference—that these authors have restricted themselves to showing the effect of obligation, without explaining clearly its content.

Some have deﬁned passive obligation and not active obligation: “Obligation,” says Pufendorf, “is a moral quality by virtue of which we are compelled, by a moral necessity, to accept or endure something.”
But he does not say in what this moral quality consists.
Grotius also uses this expression, that an action is morally necessary, to say that we are obliged to do it; but he does not in any way deﬁne obligation.

flags.fr: toutefois avec cette différence
flags.en: though sometimes with this difference
flags.note: Literally 'yet with this difference'; 'sometimes' (as if reading 'quelquefois') turns Vattel's general criticism of the earlier writers into an occasional one.

flags.fr: sans expliquer distinctement en quoi elle consiste
flags.en: without explaining clearly its content
flags.note: Literally 'without explaining distinctly what it consists in'; 'clearly' loses the Wolffian sense of 'distinct' (analysed into its marks, i.e. defined), which is the point of Vattel's complaint.

flags.fr: à faire, recevoir, ou souffrir quelque chose
flags.en: to accept or endure something
flags.note: Literally 'to do, receive, or suffer something'; the English drops 'to do', the chief item in Pufendorf's definition of obligation as quoted by Vattel.

sents: Those who only have extremely confused ideas of all this will perhaps object that it is duty which creates obligation, and that we are obliged to undertake certain actions because they are in line with our duty , and abstain from others because they conﬂict with it.
Nothing is more common than this way of speaking; it is why it matters to throw light on the problem, although, as we shall see, it consists only of pure gibberish.
Let us see therefore what is this duty on which obligation is based.
notes: A thing is morally necessary when it cannot fail to happen, given the nature of the intelligent being which produces it; just as it is said that a thing is physically necessary when it cannot fail to happen, given the nature of the physical agent that creates it.
See Wolff, Phil. Pract. Univ., part I, §cxviii.
Idem, §cxix.
Droit de la nature et des gens, book 1, ch. i, §xxi.
De Jure Belli ac Pacis, l. I, c. 1, §x.

sents: Our duty is no more than the way in which we must determine or direct our actions so that they are good and right.

Now, a free action is good or right when it has its justiﬁcation in the essence and attributes of the being that produces it, that is to say, when a reason or explanation can be given through the essence and attributes of this being as to why his action has had to be so and not otherwise.

This recalls what we have said (§VI) about the match or mismatch of actions with the essence of the nature of man and of things, which creates the foundation of natural law and the source of the laws that compose it.
It still remains to ﬁnd out the nature of the obligation we are under to live according to our duty , and, in consequence, the objection we have just witnessed is only empty verbiage.

The same outcome will hold good if the term duty is considered in another sense, according to which particular duty is an action decided on in accordance with law, in such a way that we are compelled to resolve on it in this way.
For in this sense, it is obligation, which constitutes duty , and so, it does not stem from duty.

flags.fr: sa raison suffisante
flags.en: its justiﬁcation
flags.note: Literally 'its sufficient reason'; 'justification' hides the Leibnizian-Wolffian principle of sufficient reason on which Vattel's definition of a good action rests, and shifts it from explanation to vindication.

flags.fr: Ce qui revient à ce que nous avons dit
flags.en: This recalls what we have said
flags.note: Literally 'which amounts to what we have said'; Vattel claims that the sufficient-reason criterion is equivalent to the agreement of actions with the nature of man (§6), whereas 'recalls' makes it a mere reminder.

flags.fr: de la convenance  ou disconvenance des actions
flags.en: the match or mismatch of actions
flags.note: Literally 'the agreement or disagreement (fitness or unfitness) of actions'; 'match or mismatch' obscures the technical term (Wolff's consensus, Burlamaqui's convenance) on which Vattel grounds natural law.

flags.fr: avec l'essence & la nature de l'homme
flags.en: with the essence of the nature of man
flags.note: Literally 'with the essence and the nature of man'; the English collapses Vattel's paired terms essence and nature into 'the essence of the nature', altering the standard by which actions are judged.

flags.fr: en tant que nous sommes obligés à la déterminer de cette maniere
flags.en: in such a way that we are compelled to resolve on it in this way
flags.note: Literally 'insofar as we are obliged to determine it in this way'; the English turns the defining condition (it is obligation that constitutes duty, as the next sentence says) into a consequence, and again renders 'obligés' as 'compelled'.

sents: Mr. Barbeyrac in his notes on Grotius and Pufendorf provides no deﬁnition of obligation at all; except that, while saying that there is no obligation without a superior, he makes it appear that we are subject to the will of a superior, which compels us to bring our conduct into conformity with this superior’s laws.
But it is plainly a confusion to interpret obligation as dependency or submission.
We still have to explain why this dependence binds us; why we must preserve this submission.
If we ask this learned man, “Why must we obey a superior?” he will not reply, “Because we are obliged to.”
This would be to say nothing and to explain like with like.
Will he say that it is because this obedience is just, in conformity with the rules of order, or because this superior can punish us if we rebel against him?

But in that case he is citing to us the motives which are linked to this action of obedience, and he falls back on our deﬁnition, according to which obligation is the connection or link of motive with action.
notes: In Latin rectae. The correctness of an action, rectitudo, means what is understood by the words right, just, good, praiseworthy, etc.
The difference which exists between free actions, in respect to this correctness, is what is called the morality of actions.
Wolff, Theol. nat., part I, §dccccl.

flags.fr: il  l'a fait envisager comme une dépendance où nous sommes de la volonté d'un supérieur
flags.en: he makes it appear that we are subject to the will of a superior
flags.note: Literally 'he makes it [obligation] appear as a dependence in which we stand on the will of a superior'; the English drops the identification of obligation with dependence, which is exactly what Vattel attacks in the next sentence.

flags.fr: expliquer idem per idem
flags.en: explain like with like
flags.note: Literally 'explain the same by the same', i.e. a circular explanation; 'like with like' suggests explaining by something similar and blunts the charge of tautology.

sents: Now this deﬁnition is adequately established if the ﬁrst principle of obligation can be found which binds us to the observance of natural law, to a principle which is truly primary, which does not stem from any other.

Then it is clear that we can only ﬁnd it in a general motive which moves us, without drawing its effectiveness from any other, and which, in contrast, all the others relate to as branches or subsidiary motives, which draw all their strength from this common source.

flags.fr: Maintenant que cette définition est suffisamment établie, sie l'on veut trouver le prémier principe de l'obligation
flags.en: Now this deﬁnition is adequately established if the ﬁrst principle of obligation can be found
flags.note: Literally 'now that this definition is sufficiently established, if one wants to find the first principle of obligation'; the English makes the definition's validity conditional on finding the first principle, misrepresenting the order of the argument.

sents: Given that motives act on us in accordance with our desires, to discover what we are looking for, we must see if there is in our soul an affection or essential and basic desire, which does not derive from another, and on which all the others rely.

We do not need a long period of reﬂection to convince us that there is no inclination, desire, or affection more essential to us, or more basic and general, than self-love, which causes us to desire and seek for our happiness or the perfection of our condition, whether internal or external, i.e., the perfection of our soul, the well-being of our body, and the prosperity of our fortune.

flags.fr: Les motifs n'agissant sur nous qu'en vertu de nos désirs, de nos inclinations
flags.en: Given that motives act on us in accordance with our desires
flags.note: Literally 'motives acting on us only by virtue of our desires, our inclinations'; the English drops 'only' (and 'inclinations'), weakening the premise that motives work solely through desire, from which Vattel infers that the first motive must be a primitive desire.

sents: That being so, the most general motive that inﬂuences us, this basic motive which stems from no other, can only be what relies on this general and basic inclination.
Now, what is this motive, which stems from selflove or our desire for happiness?
It is, for sure, our well-being, our expediency, our advantage.
Experience reveals this truth clearly to the eyes of whoever wishes to pay some attention to what takes place inside his own mind.

Let us investigate carefully, let us examine attentively the way in which our wishes are formed, and we shall see that we never determine on an action through the perception of some beneﬁt that we think we perceive in it, whether for perfection or peace and the pleasure of our soul, or for the well-being of our body, or for the proﬁt of our fortune.
Every motive returns, ultimately, to real or perceived expediency.

But we must observe in passing that if our greatest good comprises the perfection of our soul, then the motives that relate to it—for example, those which derive from obedience owed to a being such as God, independent of all fear, beauty, and virtue—these motives, I say, may be considered as the noblest with good reason.
After them, those that are concerned with the good of the body are the most rational; ﬁnally, the motives that provide us with the condition of our fortune take the third place.

flags.fr: le motif le plus général qui nous détermine
flags.en: the most general motive that inﬂuences us
flags.note: Literally 'the most general motive that determines us'; 'influences' weakens Vattel's claim that motives determine the will, on which his definition of obligation rests.

flags.fr: Et par là-jentens tout ce qui peut véritablement contribuer à la perfection de notre Ame, à cel-  le de notre Corps & à notre bien-être dans ce monde, mais sur tous, & par préférence à toute autre chose, ce qui contribuë à la perfection de notre Ame, qui est notre grand & vrai bien.
flags.note: Literally 'and by this I mean all that can truly contribute to the perfection of our soul, of our body and to our well-being in this world, but above all ... what contributes to the perfection of our soul, which is our great and true good'; the English drops Vattel's definition of utility as chiefly perfection of the soul, on which his reply to Barbeyrac in §30 depends.

flags.fr: Voilà la vraie Définition de l'utile.
flags.note: Literally 'This is the true definition of the useful'; the English never signals that Vattel has just given a technical definition of utility.

flags.fr: C'est donc notre utilité qui est le principe général & primitif de toutes nos déterminations.
flags.note: Literally 'It is therefore our utility that is the general and primitive principle of all our determinations'; the explicit conclusion is missing, so 'this truth' in the next English sentence refers back only to the list of our goods.

flags.fr: nous ne nous déterminons jamais à une action, que par la vue de quelque bien
flags.en: we never determine on an action through the perception of some beneﬁt
flags.note: Literally 'we never determine ourselves to an action except through the view of some good'; by dropping 'except' the English says the opposite, that we never act from the perception of a good.

flags.fr: la maniere dont se forment nos volitions
flags.en: the way in which our wishes are formed
flags.note: Literally 'the way our volitions are formed'; 'wishes' replaces acts of the will with mere desires, blurring the analysis of how the will is determined.

flags.fr: notre plus grand bien consistant dans la perfection de notre ame
flags.en: if our greatest good comprises the perfection of our soul
flags.note: Literally 'our greatest good consisting in the perfection of our soul', stated as fact; the English turns Vattel's premise into a mere condition ('if').

flags.fr: indépendamment de toute crainte, de la beauté de la vertu
flags.en: independent of all fear, beauty, and virtue
flags.note: Literally '[motives] taken from the obedience due to God independently of all fear, [and] from the beauty of virtue, etc.'; the English makes obedience independent of 'beauty and virtue' and so drops the beauty of virtue from Vattel's list of the noblest motives.

flags.fr: les motifs que nous fournit l'état de notre fortune
flags.en: the motives that provide us with the condition of our fortune
flags.note: Literally 'the motives that the state of our fortune furnishes us'; the English inverts subject and object.

flags.fr: On peut voir ce que nous disons là-dessus, dans la lettre sur les sentimens désintéressés, page .... de ce recueil.
flags.note: Literally 'see what we say on this in the letter on disinterested sentiments, page ... of this collection'; the cross-reference, which ties this ranking of motives to Vattel's piece on disinterested love in Le loisir philosophique, is missing (probably absent from the 1863 reprint).

sents: If our expediency and our well-being are therefore the predominant motivation, the most basic motive that drives us, we must conclude that this good, this expediency, is the ﬁrst principle of all obligation, and in particular of the obligation to keep to natural law.

There is no doubt that our expediency is linked to this observance, for natural law is a science that teaches us what is naturally good or bad in man (§III); and the natural laws that comprise this law only prescribe some actions and forbid others as a result of the harmony or disharmony of these actions with our nature and the nature of things (§VI).

flags.fr: Notre utilité
flags.en: our expediency
flags.note: Literally 'our utility'; 'expediency' suggests short-term, morally dubious advantage, the 'crude utility' Vattel rejects in §30, and the translation switches between 'expediency', 'self-interest', 'interest' and 'usefulness' for this one key term.

flags.fr: notre bien
flags.en: our well-being
flags.note: Literally 'our good' (bien); 'well-being' is the word for bien-être, and a few words later 'ce bien' is rendered 'this good', so the term is unstable.

flags.fr: le motif le plus général
flags.en: the predominant motivation
flags.note: Literally 'the most general motive', the one from which all others derive; 'predominant' turns a claim about logical priority into one about strength.

flags.fr: étant donc
flags.en: If our expediency and our well-being are therefore
flags.note: Literally 'our utility, our good, being therefore the most general motive', a conclusion drawn from §21; the English 'If' makes it a hypothesis.

flags.fr: ce qui est naturellement bon ou mauvais à l'homme
flags.en: what is naturally good or bad in man
flags.note: Literally 'what is naturally good or bad for man'; 'in man' loses the point that natural law teaches what serves or harms man, which is why utility is joined to its observance.

flags.fr: les loix naturelles qui constituent ce droit
flags.en: the natural laws that comprise this law
flags.note: Literally 'the natural laws that make up this right [droit]'; rendering both droit and loi as 'law' collapses Vattel's distinction between the body of natural right and the laws composing it.

sents: Man is a social animal; society is natural to him; indeed, it is even essential to him if he is to pass his life happily.

From this observation the judicious Grotius adopted the sociability of man as the foundation of natural law; and that is very reasonable provided that we do not take it as the ﬁrst principle of obligation, but only as the next principle from which the duty derives for all men to follow the laws which must govern the natural society which exists among them, and without which they cannot survive.

flags.fr: pour le principe prochain
flags.en: as the next principle
flags.note: 'Principe prochain' is the technical 'proximate principle' (so rendered in §29), opposed to the first principle; 'next' obscures the term.

flags.fr: duquel on déduit l'obligation
flags.en: from which the duty derives
flags.note: Literally 'from which one deduces the obligation'; 'duty' breaks the parallel with 'first principle of obligation' in the same sentence and blurs Vattel's distinction between obligation and duty.

flags.fr: & sans lesquelles elle ne peut subsister
flags.en: and without which they cannot survive
flags.note: Literally 'and without which it [natural society] cannot subsist'; the English makes men, not society, unable to survive without the laws.

sents: Each individual has as a general and overriding motive his own self-interest, and this motive creates the obligation to which he is liable: it is the unvarying principle of his decisions, against which it would be absurd to claim that he could be made to act.

But if society is useful and even necessary to him, and this society is unable to subsist without laws or general rules observed by all its members, he is obliged, by virtue of his own expediency, to follow them.
He ought not even consider sacriﬁcing them to an immediate advantage, because they are what guarantee him peaceful enjoyment of all his other goods.

flags.fr: motif général & prémier
flags.en: general and overriding motive
flags.note: Literally 'general and first motive' (first in order); 'overriding' turns priority of derivation into strength.

flags.fr: son utilité propre
flags.en: his own self-interest
flags.note: Literally 'his own utility'; the next sentence renders the same idea 'his own expediency', and 'self-interest' evokes intérêt or amour-propre rather than Vattel's broad utility.

flags.fr: Mais la société lui étant utile
flags.en: But if society is useful
flags.note: Literally 'but society being useful ... to him'; Vattel asserts this, while the English makes it conditional.

flags.fr: Il ne doit même pas balancer à leur sacrifier dans des cas particuliers un avantage présent
flags.en: He ought not even consider sacriﬁcing them to an immediate advantage
flags.note: Literally 'he must not even hesitate to sacrifice to them [the laws], in particular cases, a present advantage'; the English reverses what is sacrificed to what and drops 'in particular cases'.

sents: That is the foundation of civil laws and the principle of the submission that we owe to them.
Men, who are required by their needs to form individual societies, will deﬁnitely not give up their own selfinterest and expediency on entering them.
On the contrary, it was doubtless on account of this very beneﬁt that they each decided to make these commitments.

But readily perceiving that such a host of evils and disadvantages might arise among people so often blinded by or taken up with their passions (if every individual had the freedom to decide, in particular instances, what was the best course of action for him), they understood that they had to establish laws that were sufﬁcient to guarantee the happiness of society.
They adjusted them, so far as was possible for a majority, to the interest of each member.

Everyone felt that these laws, if they were to achieve the desired effect, must be observed religiously; that exceptions could not be made from them without weakening or destroying them, and that therefore on this occasion they had to sacriﬁce an immediate advantage to a greater good, since laws are the basis of our peace and security.
That is the true principle of the obligation we have to observe them, a principle to which all men subject themselves without difﬁculty.

flags.fr: ne renoncérent certainement pas
flags.en: will deﬁnitely not give up
flags.note: Literally 'certainly did not renounce' (past tense, in Vattel's account of how civil societies were formed); the English turns the historical claim into a general prediction.

flags.fr: à son bien
flags.en: their own selfinterest
flags.note: Literally 'his own good' (bien); rendered 'self-interest' while 'utilité propre' in the same phrase becomes 'expediency', so both key terms shift.

flags.fr: de ce qui lui est le plus avantageux
flags.en: what was the best course of action for him
flags.note: Literally 'what is most advantageous to him'; the English loses the point that each individual would judge by his own advantage.

flags.fr: dans leur généralité
flags.en: so far as was possible for a majority
flags.note: Literally 'they adapted them, as far as possible in their generality [as general rules], to the utility of each member'; 'for a majority' introduces a majoritarian idea absent from the French.

flags.fr: à l'utilité de chaque membre
flags.en: to the interest of each member
flags.note: Literally 'to the utility of each member'; 'interest' is yet another rendering of Vattel's key term utilité.

flags.fr: il faut leur sacrifier dans l'occasion un avantage présent
flags.en: on this occasion they had to sacriﬁce an immediate advantage
flags.note: Literally 'one must sacrifice to them, when the occasion arises, a present advantage', a standing rule; the English makes it a one-time sacrifice by the founders 'on this occasion'.

flags.fr: l'on ne peut y faire soi-même des exceptions
flags.en: exceptions could not be made from them
flags.note: Literally 'one cannot oneself make exceptions to them'; dropping 'oneself' loses the point that individuals may not exempt themselves.

sents: The view that I established (§XXI) on the principle of obligation is not new, and I ﬁnd in a note of Mr. Barbeyrac, on the great work of Pufendorf, a passage in which I see with a particular pleasure, that a learned Englishman shared exactly the same views: “According to him, duty or obligation, in respect of man, can only be a reason or motive put forward in an appropriate manner, which makes him decide to choose or to prefer one way of acting over another; and this reason or motive can only be the avoidance or acquisition of a very high degree of unhappiness or happiness, which cannot be avoided or gained by acting in another manner.
He does not acknowledge any other obligation—or if there be some other type, he believes that by examining it carefully it will be seen to resolve itself into the same kind.”
Thus Mr. Bernard expresses the thoughts of Mr. Gastrell: which are precisely in line with what I have tried to establish.
notes: Book I, ch. vi, §v, note 4.

flags.fr: détermine nécessairement à choisir
flags.en: makes him decide to choose
flags.note: Literally 'which necessarily determines him to choose'; dropping 'necessarily' removes the necessity that makes this a definition of obligation.

flags.fr: un plus grand degré
flags.en: a very high degree
flags.note: Literally 'a greater degree of misery to avoid or of felicity to gain [than] one can avoid or gain by acting otherwise'; the comparative becomes an absolute 'very high degree', losing the comparison between courses of action on which the definition rests.

sents: But let us see what Mr. Barbeyrac puts forward in the same note: “The motive for obligation, or what brings about most effective compliance with it, should not be confused with the foundation of obligation or the reason why we are absolutely required to do one thing or another.
This reason is nothing other than the will of a superior, whose power, in relation to our own good or evil, then stimulates our will to determine our present duty.”
The whole problem between this learned commentator and ourselves derives from the fact that he does not deﬁne obligation as we have done (§XVIII).
Expediency, he says, is the motive for obligation, it is not the foundation: we are required to obey a superior.
But we may ask him: what, therefore, is the foundation of obligation, and for what reason am I to obey a superior?
You will tell me that it is my duty to obey him because I am dependent on him.
That still does not enlighten me.
I continue: why must I respect this dependency?
Why must I fulﬁll my duty?
And if I violate it, what will happen?
You will punish me, you will say.
And there we have the motive that creates my obligation to this duty: by breaking with it, I bring harm to myself.
But if I could avoid the punishment, would this transgression still be an offense?
Yes, you say—and why?
Because I must obey a superior who has a legitimate authority over me: my disobedience would be a bad act.
But why should I not commit an evil act when it will draw down no punishment upon me?
You cannot respond with anything more rational than this: “In committing an evil act, an act contrary to order and reason, you depart from the perfection of your being.”
And that brings us back to my view, which bases obligation on expediency, for it is without doubt advantageous to me to be perfect.
Let us not pursue any further a matter we have already touched upon (§XVIII).
notes: Nouvelles de la Re´publique des Lettres, April 1700, p. 408. [[In 1699 the French Reformed theologian Jacques Bernard began a continuation of Pierre Bayle’s Nouvelles de la Re´publique des Lettres (1684–87), which appeared until 1710.]]

flags.fr: On confond ici
flags.en: should not be confused with
flags.note: Literally 'here one confuses'; Barbeyrac charges this view (and so Vattel's) with a confusion, which the English turns into a general caution.

flags.fr: notre bonheur ou notre malheur
flags.en: our own good or evil
flags.note: Literally 'our happiness or our unhappiness'; 'good or evil' puts a moral register into a claim about the superior's power over our welfare.

flags.fr: ensorte qu'elle se détermine actuellement à ce qui est de notre devoir
flags.en: then stimulates our will to determine our present duty
flags.note: Literally 'so that it [our will] actually determines itself to what is our duty'; the English has the will 'determine our present duty', i.e. decide what duty is, and reads 'actuellement' (in fact) as 'present'.

flags.fr: il ne définit point l'obligation comme nous l'avons déja observé
flags.en: he does not deﬁne obligation as we have done
flags.note: Literally 'he does not define obligation at all, as we have already observed (§18)'; the English says he defines it differently from Vattel, not that he fails to define it.

flags.fr: Vous serez puni, me direz-vous.
flags.en: You will punish me, you will say.
flags.note: Literally 'You will be punished, you will tell me'; the English makes the opponent the one who punishes.

flags.fr: rien de raisonnable que ceci
flags.en: anything more rational than this
flags.note: Literally 'nothing reasonable except this'; Vattel claims this is the only reasonable answer, the English only that no answer is more rational.

flags.fr: une action contraire à l'ordre & „à la perfection de votre être
flags.en: an act contrary to order and reason, you depart from the perfection of your being
flags.note: The 1747 text reads 'an action contrary to order and to the perfection of your being' and leaves the sentence incomplete; 'and reason' and 'you depart from' are not in it and probably follow the 1863 text.

flags.fr: car il m'est sans doute utile d'être parfait
flags.en: for it is without doubt advantageous to me to be perfect
flags.note: Literally 'for it is doubtless useful to me to be perfect'; the argument links obligation founded on utilité to what is utile, a link lost when one is 'expediency' and the other 'advantageous'.

sents: I ﬂatter myself that by developing ideas carefully and deﬁning the meaning of terms precisely, as I have tried to do, the reader will see a way of reconciling Mr. Barbeyrac with us, and that this scholar will himself come to agree.
The will of a superior, as we have just seen, is not the ﬁrst principle or the foundation of obligation.

But it is, doubtless, a proximate principle of real substance: ﬁrstly, because disregarding the integrity inherent in the action that is prescribed for us, it is ﬁne and praiseworthy to obey a legitimate superior; and secondly, because this superior can recompense or punish us, independently of the good or evil that our action naturally entails.

And when this superior is recognized as very wise, and all-powerful, his will alone imposes on us a true obligation, even if we might not perceive the integrity of the action that he prescribes to us, or the relation that it can have in itself with our happiness.
I would go further: even if we believed we saw something harmful to us in the situation—in a word, when we do not know the reasons for the law that he gives us.

For we can relate to him; we rely on his wisdom for the integrity of the action and on his goodness for the usefulness of this very action; and it is by virtue of this legitimate trust that we can say when he prescribes a law that his will takes the place of reasons.

Moreover, while this act might be unimportant in itself, whether in terms of its integrity or our self-interest, or even contrary to it, the act becomes good and praiseworthy as soon as he prescribes it, and he is the master through his omnipotence who can attach such a reward as he considers appropriate, and compensate us a hundredfold for the harm that it will have caused us.
To God alone, as a wise and all-powerful superior, is this unlimited trust due.
But as a result the occasion for action can only exist when this sovereign legislator gives us revealed laws.

For natural laws, we only know them to be the laws of God, by the reasons for these laws—by the reasons which show their justice and expediency; so, if we do not see wise reasons for undertaking a particular action or abstaining from it, we cannot know if it is the will of God that we should do it or avoid it.

Let us recall here a passage of Mr. Barbeyrac, even if it is a little long; the reader, on comparing it with what we have just said, will see clearly the heart of the problem, how our principles cause it to vanish, and how they may serve to reconcile opinions which at ﬁrst sight seem so opposed: “The author [Grotius ] here imagines that there might be an obligation to do or not do certain things, even if he did not have to answer to anybody for his conduct.

And there is no need to be astonished that his ideas on this point are not quite in order, since we still see today, not only that the majority of philosophers and scholastic theologians, but also some authors who elsewhere are very judicious and in no way slaves to scholastic prejudice, are all obstinate in maintaining that the rules of natural law and ethics, impose in themselves an absolute obligation, independent of the will of God.
Nevertheless, some argue in a way that suggests that there is only a dispute over the meaning of words between the latter and others who are not of the same opinion.
I am going to try, albeit in a few words, to update thoroughly the state of the debate, and the basis of the disagreement I have with the author.

It is not a matter here of arguing whether by disregarding the will of an intelligent being or even the will of God our minds can discover the ideas and relations from which the rules of natural law and ethics can be deduced.

We must agree in good faith with the supporters of the view that I am combating, that the rules are effectively based on the very nature of things; that they are in conformity with the order that we conceive as necessary to the beauty of the universe; that there is a certain proportion or lack of proportion, aptitude or unsuitability between the majority of actions and their objects, which makes sure that we ﬁnd beauty in some and ugliness in others.
But from that alone it does not follow that anyone is properly obliged to do or not do one thing or another.

The ﬁtness or unsuitability, which we can call the natural morality of actions, is indeed a reason which can cause action or its refusal, but it is not a reason which imposes an absolute requirement, such as the idea of obligation implies.
This necessity can only come from a superior, i.e., from an intelligent being outside ourselves, who has the power to restrict our freedom and to prescribe rules of conduct for us.
For proof, here is my reasoning.
If there were some obligation, independent of the will of a superior, either the nature of things would have to impose it or our own reason.
The very nature of things could not impose any obligation on us, in any real sense.

That there may be a harmonious or disharmonious relationship between our ideas, this alone does not require a recognition of this relationship—something further is required to compel us to make our acts and life conform.
Nor can reason by itself place us under an indispensable necessity to follow the ideas of harmony or disharmony that it sets before our eyes as based on the nature of things.”
(I do not copy the proof that the author gives of it, which is found word for word in his reply to the Judgment of Mr. Leibniz, which I shall look at shortly.
Let us move on to his conclusion.)

“From all these points I conclude that the maxims of reason, however congruent they may be with the nature of things, and with the makeup of our being, are in no way binding, until this very same reason has revealed to us the Author of existence and of the nature of things, who gives the force of law to these maxims by his will, and imposes on us an indispensable necessity of conforming to them by virtue of the right he has to limit our liberty as he considers appropriate, and to set such boundaries for the faculties he has given us as seem good to him.

It is true that God can ordain nothing contrary to the ideas of harmony or disharmony with which reason furnishes us in certain acts; but that does not alter the fact that the obligation to regulate ourselves according to those ideas stems uniquely from his will.
It matters not whether this will is arbitrary or not; it is always the will alone which imposes the necessity.

Finally, a proof that the will of God is the source of every duty and obligation, lies in that fact that when those who have a religion, adopt the rules of virtue and the maxims of natural law, they must do so, not chieﬂy because they recognize that these rules are in conformity with the natural and unvarying ideas of order, harmony, and justice, but rather because God, their sovereign master, wishes them to follow the rules in their conduct.”
A charming proof, which precisely deﬁnes what is at issue.
But perhaps there is a path of reconciliation between us.
We reply to all this reasoning that men would be obliged to follow natural laws even by setting aside the will of God, because they are praiseworthy and useful.

But this will undoubtedly adds a great weight to this obligation: it is a very legitimate and solid foundation although this foundation is not a basic principle since it derives itself from another from whom it draws its strength—I mean, our self-interest.
Will not the learned commentator on Grotius be obliged to agree, and will he not admit that his note is useless against a similar system?

He adds, “that ultimately it would otherwise be fairly purposeless that God prescribed anything (to men ), since they would already be held to it: the will and authority of God would only in this case be a kind of accessory, which would not contribute anything further than to make the obligation stronger.”
That issue, I do not consider as a difﬁculty.

In no way does it detract from the authority of God to say that everything he ordains for us in natural laws is so ﬁne and useful in itself that we would be obliged to adopt it, even if God had not ordered it.
notes: At the time of writing Mr. Barbeyrac was still alive.
“Thus will may stand in the place of reason.” Wolff, Phil. Prac. Univ., part 1, §cxxxii, in note.
Translation of On the Law of War and Peace, of Grotius, book I, ch. I, §x, no. 2, note 4.

flags.fr: la rectitude propre de l'action
flags.en: the integrity inherent in the action
flags.note: Literally 'the action's own rectitude' (its moral rightness); 'integrity' is a personal quality, and the same English word later renders honnêteté, merging two terms.

flags.fr: nous pouvons nous en rapporter à lui
flags.en: we can relate to him
flags.note: 'S'en rapporter à lui' means 'we can rely on him, defer to his judgment'; 'relate to him' loses the trust in God's judgment that grounds the claim that his will takes the place of reasons.

flags.fr: indifférente en elle-même
flags.en: unimportant in itself
flags.note: Literally 'indifferent in itself' (morally neither right nor wrong); 'unimportant' loses the technical sense.

flags.fr: soit pour notre utilité
flags.en: our self-interest
flags.note: Literally 'our utility'; another switch from 'expediency' to 'self-interest' for the same term.

flags.fr: un Supérieur infiniment sage
flags.en: a wise and all-powerful superior
flags.note: Literally 'an infinitely wise and all-powerful superior'; dropping 'infinitely' weakens the reason why unlimited trust is due to God alone.

flags.fr: le cas d'agir en conséquence
flags.en: as a result the occasion for action
flags.note: Literally 'the case for acting accordingly [on such unlimited trust] can only arise when ... he gives us revealed laws'; the English makes 'the occasion for action' as such depend on revealed law.

flags.fr: nécessité indispensable de les suivre
flags.en: an absolute obligation
flags.note: Literally 'an indispensable necessity of following them'; rendering Barbeyrac's 'necessity' as 'obligation' here (elsewhere 'indispensable necessity' or 'absolute requirement') blurs the term he uses to define obligation.

flags.fr: mettre dans tout „son jour
flags.en: to update thoroughly
flags.note: 'Mettre dans tout son jour' means 'to set out in full light, to clarify'; 'update' is wrong.

flags.fr: effectivement fondées sur la nature
flags.en: effectively based on the very nature of things
flags.note: 'Effectivement' means 'really, in fact'; modern 'effectively' suggests 'in effect, virtually', weakening Barbeyrac's concession that the rules are truly grounded in nature.

flags.fr: convenance ou disconvenance
flags.en: aptitude or unsuitability
flags.note: 'Convenance ou disconvenance' (agreement or disagreement, the technical term of §6) is here 'aptitude or unsuitability', two sentences later 'fitness or unsuitability', then 'harmonious', 'harmony' and 'congruence', so the reader cannot follow one concept.

flags.fr: une raison qui peut porter à agir
flags.en: a reason which can cause action
flags.note: Literally 'a reason that can incline one to act'; 'cause' strengthens it and blurs Barbeyrac's contrast between inclining and imposing necessity.

flags.fr: ne nous engage qu'à reconnoître ce „rapport
flags.en: this alone does not require a recognition of this relationship
flags.note: Literally 'this alone obliges us only to recognize this relation'; the English denies that it obliges even to recognition, reversing Barbeyrac's distinction between assent of the mind and subjection of conduct.

flags.fr: qui pose précisément ce qui est en question
flags.en: which precisely deﬁnes what is at issue
flags.note: Literally 'which assumes precisely what is in question'; Vattel accuses Barbeyrac of begging the question, and the English loses the charge.

flags.fr: je veux dire de notre utilité
flags.en: I mean, our self-interest
flags.note: Literally 'I mean our utility'; at the conclusion of the argument 'self-interest' makes Vattel derive the force of God's will from selfishness rather than from his broad utility centred on perfection.

flags.fr: un pareil systême
flags.en: a similar system
flags.note: Literally 'such a system', i.e. Vattel's own; 'a similar system' points to some other system.

sents: Another few words about self-interest.
There is something ambiguous about this term: some deﬁne it unreasonably narrowly, and seem to mean by it a crude expediency restricted to property.

It is what gives rise to this note by Mr. Barbeyrac: “There are here two extremes to avoid: one is the work of those who by confusing integrity and expediency, and measuring this expediency according to their own particular interest, destroy thereby every idea of virtue and vice, all natural law and morality; the other, on the part of those who believing (with reason) that the practice of all the virtues, and of all the rules of natural law, is truly and infallibly to the advantage of all men in every respect, confuse this expediency with the natural integrity of actions.
The ﬁrst is only an ineluctable consequence of the other, and a feature from which we can discern what is truly honorable from what is only so in the erroneous opinion of men.

When I say, we should repay evil with good, but not good with evil; and men must obey the will of their creator, God, there is in these statements a congruence so clear and evident that, however little attention we pay to them, we cannot refrain from acquiescing, and judging the views they contain both ﬁne and honorable, without needing to think at all about the advantage which ﬂows from following them.
We are convinced from that point on that any action contrary to these maxims is a sin against reason, and we are forced to blame ourselves.
The concept of duty derives from that recognition alone, as does the rational end to follow duty.
It is true that to give full force to all these like maxims where we reveal a natural beauty and harmony, we must have been convinced of the truth of the second example I gave.

But even when everything is properly reduced to this basic rule, there is no need at all to consider the unlimited expediency which ﬂows from it as a way of perceiving the obligation we are under to conform to it.

More to the point: it is precisely not on account of this self-interest that we must currently perform what is in line with the will of God: it is solely because we admit we are his dependents and that it is ﬁne and honorable to obey him; and this would still be so even if (which would be impossible) he demanded something absolutely without purpose.

Whatever view we take of selfinterest, we must not view it simply in itself, but in terms of the product of the natural and wonderful union that the Creator has established between the duty and happiness of his creatures.
In a word, to set up expediency itself as the most real and universal foundation of moral integrity and of obligation as such, is to muddle concepts and to make what is secondary into the principal.

Let us also recognize that those who have not known about or have imperfectly understood this expediency have insufﬁciently acknowledged the intrinsic integrity of the majority of actions that conform with natural law.”

It is surely sufﬁcient to respond that when we say that self-interest provides the foundation or the principle of obligation, we are speaking of a noble and agreed expediency, which is located mainly in the observance and practice of virtue— because this observance and practice bring us closer to perfection.

I would argue that that point alone is enough to bring this reasoning tumbling down, and to lighten the difﬁculties in which the author entangles himself, from which he cannot extract himself with the help of his principles.

When we have a correct understanding of self-interest; when we have constituted it mainly in the perfection of the soul, a perfection that already deﬁnes our happiness in itself, and which reconciles us with the good will of the Creator, what danger is there in confusing the meaning of integrity with expediency ?

Furthermore—the doctrine of those who by distinguishing between integrity and expediency maintain that there are honest things that are not useful and useful ones that are not honest— is it not, as the ancients have observed, as pernicious as it is insecure?

On this point let us consider the ﬁne words of Cicero: The usage of this word has been corrupted and perverted and has gradually come to the point where, separating moral rectitude from expediency, it is accepted that a thing may be morally right without being expedient, and expedient without being morally right.
No more pernicious doctrine than this could be introduced into human life.
And so, we have heard, Socrates used to pronounce a curse upon those who ﬁrst drew a conceptual distinction between things naturally inseparable.
Now that we know what we must understand by the word expediency, let us conclude with Horace: Self-interest itself is almost the mother of justice and fairness.
notes: Translation of On the Law of Nature and Nations of Pufendorf, book II, ch. III, §x, note 6.
De ofﬁciis, book II, ch. iii.

flags.fr: l'utilité
flags.en: self-interest
flags.note: Literally 'one more word on utility'; the section examines the ambiguity of the term utilité ('ce terme'), which the English names 'self-interest' here and 'expediency' in the next sentence.

flags.fr: bornée aux biens de la terre
flags.en: restricted to property
flags.note: Literally 'limited to earthly goods'; 'property' narrows it and loses the contrast between worldly goods and the good of the soul.

flags.fr: l'honnête avec l'utile
flags.en: integrity and expediency
flags.note: 'L'honnête' is the Ciceronian honestum (the morally good); it is rendered 'integrity' here and later in this section but 'honorable' and 'honest' elsewhere, so the honestum/utile pair at the centre of the debate is obscured.

flags.fr: l'on est porté à s'en faire des reproches
flags.en: we are forced to blame ourselves
flags.note: Literally 'one is inclined to reproach oneself'; 'forced' overstates the inclination.

flags.fr: qu'on doit actuellement faire
flags.en: that we must currently perform
flags.note: 'Actuellement' here means 'actually, in fact' (in act), not 'currently'.

flags.fr: cette utilité
flags.en: this self-interest
flags.note: Literally 'this utility', referring back to the 'infinite utility' just rendered 'unlimited expediency'; switching to 'self-interest' breaks the reference.

flags.fr: absolument „inutile
flags.en: absolutely without purpose
flags.note: Literally 'absolutely useless' (without utility); 'without purpose' suggests divine purposelessness rather than lack of utility to us, which is the point of the argument.

flags.fr: Que si l'on pense à l'utilité
flags.en: Whatever view we take of selfinterest
flags.note: Literally 'if one does think of utility'; utility is again rendered 'self-interest'.

flags.fr: l'utilité même la plus réelle & la plus „universelle pour fondement
flags.en: to set up expediency itself as the most real and universal foundation
flags.note: Literally 'to make even the most real and most universal utility the foundation'; the English attaches 'most real and universal' to the foundation, so Barbeyrac seems to object only to making utility the chief foundation rather than any foundation.

flags.fr: laissé d'être frappés, & d'une maniere assez vive
flags.en: have insufﬁciently acknowledged
flags.note: Literally 'have nonetheless been struck, and quite vividly, by the intrinsic honesty of most actions'; the English says they insufficiently acknowledged it, reversing Barbeyrac's argument that the honestum is perceived without regard to utility.

flags.fr: l'utilité fait le fondement
flags.en: self-interest provides the foundation
flags.note: Literally 'utility forms the foundation'; 'self-interest' appears in the very sentence where Vattel says he means a noble utility (there rendered 'expediency'), so his reply reads as a defence of self-interest.

flags.fr: bien entendue
flags.en: agreed expediency
flags.note: 'Utilité bien entendue' means 'well-understood, rightly understood utility'; 'agreed' is wrong and loses the idea of enlightened interest.

flags.fr: dans l'observation de l'ordre & dans la pratique de la vertu
flags.en: in the observance and practice of virtue
flags.note: Literally 'in the observance of order and in the practice of virtue'; 'order', a key term linked to perfection, is dropped.

flags.fr: une juste idée de l'utilité
flags.en: a correct understanding of self-interest
flags.note: Literally 'a just idea of utility'; Vattel here defines utility as perfection of the soul, which 'self-interest' contradicts.

flags.fr: qui nous concilie la bienveillance du Créateur
flags.en: which reconciles us with the good will of the Creator
flags.note: Literally 'which wins us the Creator's goodwill'; 'reconciles us with' suggests a prior estrangement in the theological sense.

flags.fr: confondre en ce sens, l'honnête avec l'utile
flags.en: confusing the meaning of integrity with expediency
flags.note: Literally 'to confound, in this sense, the honest with the useful'; the English drops the limiting 'in this sense' (utility so understood) and speaks instead of confusing meanings.

flags.fr: séparant l'honnêteté de l'utilité
flags.en: distinguishing between integrity and expediency
flags.note: Literally 'separating honesty from utility'; Vattel attacks separating them, not distinguishing them, and the English makes him reject any distinction.

flags.fr: des choses honnêtes
flags.en: honest things
flags.note: 'Choses honnêtes' are morally right things (honesta); modern 'honest' means truthful.

flags.fr: Atque ipsa utilitas
flags.en: Self-interest itself
flags.note: Horace's 'utilitas' (utility), quoted right after Vattel says we now know what the word utility means (rendered 'expediency'), becomes 'self-interest', undercutting his point.

sents: Since we have begun to examine the reasoning that Mr. Barbeyrac develops to support his hypothesis, let us add some reﬂections on what the same scholar, at the end of his translation of the treatise On the Duties of Man and Citizen, sets up against the judgment that Mr. Leibniz had delivered on this work of Pufendorf.
This discussion will conclude by highlighting the use that we can make of our principles.

We conclude this dissertation with these remarks not with the goal of criticizing an able man, but so as to demonstrate the advantage of a precise method, and to show how by deﬁning ideas, by making them clear and deﬁning terms, we can unravel almost painlessly the debates in which many scholars have obstructed us.

“The anonymous author,” says Mr. Barbeyrac, “manifestly confuses duty with the effects or the motives for its observance; the strength that duty has in its own right with the force it exercises over the minds of men in the way that most of them are constituted.”
He should say all men here rather than most.

For Mr. Leibniz’s statement that duties have no force without motives is true of all men without exception; we have established this earlier by showing how obligation is nothing other than the link between motive and action (§XI and XII); and this philosopher, without any reference to another life, had grounded his view in the same fashion: “If we are born with such dispositions, and if we have not been brought up in such a way that we ﬁnd a great pleasure in virtue and a great distaste for vices (it is fortunate that everyone has not!), there will be nothing that can deter us from a major crime, when we will be able, through committing it, to acquire great rewards with impunity.”
And above all there will be nothing that can induce us to sacriﬁce our goods and our lives for the sake of our country, or for the support of law and justice.
For in the imaginary instance a man would have no motive to make this sacriﬁce, not even those people who can argue for the beauty of virtue.

However, Mr. Barbeyrac opposes a doctrine which seems to us so self-evident: “We are obliged,” he says, “not only not to do harm to anyone in the course of obtaining some advantage for ourselves, but also to give up on occasion our goods, honors, and even our lives, quite independent of any consideration of the life to come; and for this sole reason, that these are the duties which the wise Author of natural law and sovereign leader of the universe has imposed upon us.”
What does the term obliged mean here?

If Mr. Barbeyrac has the same concept of obligation that we have (§XI and XII), then for sure what he proposes is unsustainable: for there is no motive remaining to be linked to the action in the case in question.
If this scholar means that it is a rule of law, a maxim of the virtue of sometimes sacriﬁcing our property, etc., we would agree with him.
But how does this relate to a man who, as we imagine him here, has no taste for virtue and in no way prefers it to vice?
It is not a matter of determining the maxims of right or virtue, but of knowing the outcomes to which men will be brought or obligated in one case or another.
How will we be able to impose on them a requirement for action, without recourse to the constraints of physical force?
They are bound to these actions, says our author, by this single reason—that they are the duties which the wise Author of natural law and sovereign Leader of the universe has imposed on them.
But what purchase has this reason on a man who has no expectation of this sovereign Legislator, and who has no love for virtue, and supports as well the hypothesis against which we are reasoning?
notes: Ibid., book III, ch. iii. [[Translations taken from Loeb edition edited by Walter Miller (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1913).]]
Satires 3, book 1.
Mr. Leibniz.
P. 444. I use the 4th edition published in Amsterdam in 1718. [[See note 16.]]

flags.fr: de plus savans que nous se sont embarrassés
flags.en: many scholars have obstructed us
flags.note: Literally 'in which men more learned than we have entangled themselves'; the English makes scholars obstruct Vattel and drops his modest comparison.

flags.fr: en les rendant distinctes
flags.en: by making them clear
flags.note: Literally 'by making them distinct', the Leibniz-Wolff technical term as opposed to merely clear ideas; 'clear' changes the concept.

flags.fr: ensorte que ce Philosophe étoit fondé  à soutenir, que sans la considération d'une autre vie
flags.en: and this philosopher, without any reference to another life, had grounded his view in the same fashion
flags.note: Literally 'so that this philosopher was justified in maintaining that, without the consideration of another life, [nothing will deter from crime]'; the English makes Leibniz argue 'without reference to another life' instead of asserting that without an afterlife nothing deters crime.

flags.fr: si l'on n'est „né avec de telles dispositions
flags.en: If we are born with such dispositions
flags.note: Literally 'if one is not born with such dispositions'; dropping the negative makes those born with a love of virtue the ones nothing can deter from crime.

flags.fr: (bonheur que tout le „monde n'a pas)
flags.en: (it is fortunate that everyone has not!)
flags.note: Literally '(a good fortune that not everyone has)'; the English says it is fortunate that not everyone has such a disposition or upbringing.

flags.fr: pas même ceux que peut fournir la beauté de la vertu
flags.en: not even those people who can argue for the beauty of virtue
flags.note: Literally 'not even those [motives] that the beauty of virtue can furnish'; the English replaces the beauty of virtue as a motive with 'people who can argue' for it.

flags.fr: indépendamment de la „vûe des récompenses & des peines „d'une autre vie
flags.en: quite independent of any consideration of the life to come
flags.note: Literally 'independently of the prospect of the rewards and punishments of another life'; the English widens this to any consideration of the afterlife and drops the sanctions that are the point at issue.

flags.fr: une maxime de la vertu , de sacrifier quelquefois ses biens
flags.en: a maxim of the virtue of sometimes sacriﬁcing our property
flags.note: Literally 'a maxim of virtue to sacrifice one's goods sometimes'; the English invents a particular 'virtue of sacrificing'.

flags.fr: une espèce de nécessité d'agir
flags.en: a requirement for action
flags.note: Literally 'a kind of necessity to act' (moral, not physical, necessity); 'requirement' loses the concept of necessity central to Vattel's definition of obligation.

flags.fr: ainsi que porte l'hypothèse sur laquelle nous raisonnons
flags.en: and supports as well the hypothesis against which we are reasoning
flags.note: Literally 'as the hypothesis on which we are reasoning supposes'; the English makes the man support a hypothesis that Vattel is reasoning against.

sents: “Which of these two moral outlooks, I ask you,” adds Mr. Barbeyrac, “is the most pure, noble, and conformable to the ideas of the wise pagan authors who have distinguished so clearly between integrity and expediency ?”
Without getting into an argument about the epithets pure and noble, let us ask in turn what is the goal of those who teach natural law and ethics?
Is it not to bring men to an observance of justice and to the practice of virtue?
Which moral system is therefore the most reasonable and useful?
The one that, based on the nature of man, bears him toward virtue through considering his best interests?
Or the one that is so pure and noble that it is outside our reach and entirely useless as an inﬂuence on our will?
As for the ideas of the wise pagan authors, we have seen that the wisest had sharply turned away from a clear separation of integrity and expediency.
Socrates, says Cicero, execrated those who were the ﬁrst in their opinions to have separated things that nature had closely united.

flags.fr: l'honnête & l'utile
flags.en: integrity and expediency
flags.note: Literally 'the honest (honestum) and the useful (utile)'; 'integrity' narrows the honestum to a personal quality and 'expediency' gives utile a pejorative sense that prejudges Vattel's thesis that the useful and the honest coincide (the same 'utile' is rendered 'useful' in k2).

flags.fr: étoient bien éloignés de si bien distinguer entre l'honnête & l'utile
flags.en: had sharply turned away from a clear separation of integrity and expediency
flags.note: Literally 'the wisest were very far from distinguishing so neatly between the honest and the useful'; the English turns a statement that they did not draw the distinction into an active, deliberate rejection of it.

sents: Mr. Barbeyrac continues: “But how does the reasoning of our anonymous author match up with what he says here, that there is a level of natural law which can exist even in the case of an atheist ?
And also with what he argues later (§XV) that there would be some natural obligation, even if someone argued that there is no Divinity?”
The anonymous author, or Mr. Leibniz, has not contradicted himself.
He argues (p. 445) that to neglect consideration of a life to come, which has an inseparable link with divine Providence, is to destroy several duties of life.

He does not say that it would destroy all of them: on the contrary, he concedes that there would still be a large number of duties for an atheist, because there are, in fact, several where the reasons or motives which bind us, reside in their expediency, even in respect of this life; and an atheist can also in several instances readily ﬁnd sufﬁcient motives in the beauty of virtue alone.
Mr. Barbeyrac, at the same time as he accuses his adversary of a contradiction, cannot prevent himself stating in the two following pages (446 & 447), what destroys this alleged contradiction.
We can read these pages, and I pass on to another passage.
notes: From the cited [[1718 fourth French]] edition of On the Duties of Man and the Citizen, in which the “Judgment of an Anonymous Author” (Mr. Leibniz) has been interpolated with the reﬂections of the editor.

flags.fr: quand même on accorderoit „qu'il n'y a point de divinité
flags.en: even if someone argued that there is no Divinity
flags.note: Literally 'even if one were to grant that there is no Deity' (the Grotian etiamsi daremus concession); 'someone argued' turns a hypothetical concession into an opponent's assertion.

flags.fr: qu'il soutient encore plus bas
flags.en: (§XV)
flags.note: The French says only 'what he maintains further down'; the section reference (§XV) is not in the 1747 text and is an editorial addition, possibly following the 1863 text.

flags.fr: se trouvent dans leur utilité
flags.en: reside in their expediency
flags.note: Literally 'lie in their utility'; 'expediency' suggests opportunism and misrepresents Leibniz's and Vattel's point that the reasons for many duties lie in their real usefulness even for this life.

sents: “There is no middle course: either the obligation of the rules of justice among men is absolutely independent of the Divinity, and based uniquely on the very nature of things, as is the case with the principles of arithmetic and geometry, or it is not based on the nature of things in any respect.”
And why might there be no middle ground ?

There is one to be sure, and here it is: obligation derives from the very nature of things, but the Divinity is among the number of these things, whose nature determines the rules of justice and injustice, and provides the motives which constitute obligation.
Moreover, we have noted earlier (§XXIX) that the will of God is also an immediate and very powerful principle of obligation.

It is not difﬁcult to prove what Mr. Leibniz advances— that the opinion of those who derive every right from the will of a superior is devoid of foundation, and that we need always to come back to the nature of things.

When a man who has no other lights but those of reason identiﬁes that one action is good and that another is bad, what proof does he have that it is the will of God that creates the former and is absent from the latter?
His reason, you will say, teaches him that God wishes for all that is good.
Very well.

But this response itself demonstrates that the intrinsic quality of the action is already a reason to prefer it, disregarding the will of God; and that the very will of God orders itself according to this reason.

This will is therefore not the ﬁrst principle, the foundation of the preference that places the good above the bad: it adds only a great weight to reason derived from the nature of things; and when it is clearly known, it must take the place of everything, and provide us with a sufﬁcient reason to determine our action without further investigation, on the particular merits of the prescribed end (§XXIX).

flags.fr: ceux qui font naître tout droit de la volonté d'un Supérieur
